summary:
Six evals were run; two of them ("negative-training-pending" and "negative-live-fault-is-it-aws") were marked should_trigger:false and fully skipped for expected-output, assertions, metrics, comparison, and consistency — both variants only have a trigger_fired signal there (100% for both), so no comparative data exists for those two. The remaining four evals provide the substantive comparison.

Across these four evals, with_skill met the expected output in 4/4 cases (3 at high confidence, 1 at 100%/high), while without_skill met it in only 1/4 cases (bt-jsonl-format, at high confidence) and failed to meet it in the other three (serverless-cold-start-provisioned-concurrency, sv-async-no-notification, sv-async-payload-limit), with medium or unspecified confidence on those failures. This is a consistent pattern favoring with_skill on the expected-output measure, though it rests on LLM-judged confidence that is "medium" in several of the failing cases for without_skill rather than uniformly "high."

Per-assertion results show a similar pattern:
- In serverless-cold-start-provisioned-concurrency, with_skill passed 5/5 assertions and without_skill passed 2/5 — three assertions (cold-start explanation, no-datapoints-vs-zero distinction, command-not-API change) passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill, while two assertions (ServerlessConfig usage, no account ID exposure) passed for both.
- In bt-jsonl-format, with_skill passed 3/4 and without_skill passed 2/4; two assertions passed for both (JSONL distinction, split-type explanation), one (concrete fix) passed only for with_skill, and one (no account ID exposure) failed for both variants — indicating that specific assertion is not being satisfied regardless of variant and may need attention.
- In sv-async-no-notification and sv-async-payload-limit, without_skill has no assertion data at all (marked null/inconclusive) because its expected-output check failed before assertions could be scored, so no real with_skill-vs-without_skill comparison is possible for these two evals' assertions — only with_skill's own pass rates (3/4 in each) are available.

On quality comparison, only bt-jsonl-format had an evaluated pair, and it favored with_skill across all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) at high confidence; the other three evals had their quality comparison skipped (0 pairs evaluated), so quality differences are largely unmeasured outside that one eval.

Runtime and cost consistently favor without_skill: it ran notably faster and cheaper in every eval (e.g., 34s/$0.28 vs 10s/$0.08 for serverless-cold-start; 17s/$0.15 vs 0s/$0.00 and 20s/$0.17 vs 0s/$0.00 for the two sv-async evals; 27s/$0.23 vs 5s/$0.05 for bt-jsonl-format). Note that without_skill's 0s/$0.00 runtime in the sv-async evals likely reflects that it produced no substantive output to be scored (consistent with its expected-output failures there), rather than an efficient full response.

Output consistency (run-to-run variation) was not measurable in any eval — all consistency fields are null, so no conclusions can be drawn about stability across repeated runs for either variant.

Overall, the data shows a tradeoff: with_skill more reliably met expected outputs and satisfied individual assertions across these four evals, and was favored on quality in the one eval where quality was scored, while without_skill was consistently faster and cheaper but frequently did not produce output meeting the expected criteria, and in two evals its lack of output prevented any assertion-level comparison. One assertion (account ID exposure) failed for both variants in bt-jsonl-format, indicating a shared gap rather than a difference between variants. Two of the six evals contributed no comparative data due to being skipped by design.

serverless-cold-start-provisioned-concur.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task. The trigger behavior under test fired successfully (1/1).

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%, high confidence), while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%, medium confidence). Since this rests on a single task instance, it's a single data point rather than a broad trend, but the confidence ratings behind it are reasonably solid for with_skill (high) and more moderate for without_skill (medium).

Assertions (5 total, each evaluated once per variant): with_skill passed all 5 (100%), without_skill passed 2 of 5 (40%). Breaking this down by assertion:
- Two assertions passed for both variants: using the given ServerlessConfig context correctly before recommending a change, and not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID. These do not differentiate the variants since both handled them successfully.
- Three assertions passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill: explaining that on-demand serverless scaling to zero causes an expected cold start after idle, distinguishing "no datapoints" from a "measured zero" when reading the cold-start signal, and presenting the Provisioned Concurrency change as an operator-run command rather than invoking a mutating API directly. These three failures are where the variants diverge most clearly, and they touch on both technical accuracy (cold-start/datapoint reasoning) and operational safety (not auto-mutating infrastructure).
- No assertion failed for both variants, so there's no evidence here of a universally weak assertion or behavior.

Metrics: with_skill took ~34s and cost ~$0.28 per run, versus without_skill's ~10s and ~$0.08 — with_skill ran about 24s longer and cost roughly 3.5x more. Context window utilization was low for both (6.4% vs 4.6%), with no compaction events for either. This is a case where the variant with notably higher assertion pass rates and expected-output match also took longer and cost more — a tradeoff between speed/cost and correctness on this task, not a one-sided regression.

Quality comparison: no comparable pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no independent quality-judgment signal to weigh here — this dimension is effectively absent data.

Output consistency: not measured for either variant (null for both), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, for this single task, with_skill satisfied the expected output and all assertions tested, while without_skill failed the expected-output check and three of five assertions (notably around cold-start reasoning and safe/non-mutating operational guidance), but did so faster and at lower cost. With only one task instance and no quality-comparison or consistency data available, this should be read as a narrow, single-sample finding rather than a broad performance verdict.

This makes the "0/1" result more a sign of a missing/empty output than a substantive quality comparison, and should be read with caution.

Overall: This single eval provides very limited comparative signal. The data pattern (zero cost/runtime and null assertions for without_skill) suggests without_skill likely failed to produce an output for this task rather than genuinely underperforming on content quality, so the "expected output" gap should not be read as a clear quality verdict. For with_skill, the one substantive finding is a real assertion failure around account-ID exposure alongside three passes, but confidence markers (inconclusive pattern) temper how much weight to place on this single data point. bt-jsonl-format.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about diagnosing a line-delimited JSON/record-splitting issue in an AWS data pipeline. The trigger behavior under test fired successfully (1/1).

Expected output: Both without_skill and with_skill fully met the expected output (1/1, 100%), with high-confidence judgments on both sides — this dimension shows no difference between them, though it is based on just a single task so the finding is not broad.

Assertions (4 total, each evaluated once):
- Two assertions passed for both variants: identifying the line-delimited JSON requirement as distinct from a single JSON document, and explaining how split type/content type governs record division. These don't differentiate the variants.
- One assertion ("gives a concrete fix to the input file or job configuration") passed for with_skill (high confidence) but failed for without_skill (medium confidence) — this is the one place the two variants diverged on correctness.
- One assertion ("No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed") failed for both variants, suggesting this specific check or the underlying behavior needs attention regardless of variant.
- Net per-assertion pass rate: with_skill 3/4 (75%) vs without_skill 2/4 (50%).

Quality comparison: Across the one evaluated pair, with_skill was favored on all three criteria assessed (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with no criterion favoring without_skill and high average confidence. This is based on a single comparable pair, so it reflects one data point rather than a broad trend.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was substantially faster (~5s vs ~27s) and cheaper (~$0.05 vs ~$0.23) than with_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.4% vs 5.7%), with no compaction events for either. Neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold.

Output consistency: Not measured (null) for both variants, so no information is available on run-to-run stability.

Overall, this is a single-task evaluation with limited sample size, so all findings should be read as a single observation rather than a trend. Within that one task, with_skill showed higher assertion pass rate and was favored on quality criteria, while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper. One assertion (account ID exposure) failed for both variants, indicating a shared gap rather than a difference between them. No consistency data exists to confirm whether these patterns would hold across repeated runs.
